title: AirTag and Galaxy SmartTag2: Two Item Finders Near $30 for Keys, Wallets and Bags
subtitle: Small Bluetooth tags can help you find misplaced keys and bags, and they make a thoughtful gift if you match the tag to the recipient's phone.
excerpt: Apple's AirTag ($29) and Samsung's Galaxy SmartTag2 ($29.99) are two item finders priced near $30, though Apple's four-pack is $99. Here is what they do, what they cannot do, and how to pick one that fits the recipient's phone.
author: Nickel And Gadget Editors

sections.content: Most of us know the routine. You are ready to leave, your coat is on, and the car keys are nowhere to be found. You check the counter, the coat pockets and the couch cushions. Ten minutes later they turn up in yesterday's jacket.

A Bluetooth item finder is a small tag that clips to your keys or slips into a bag. Your phone can help you track it down. A single tag runs about $30, which makes it a practical gift for a parent, a grandparent or yourself, as long as you pick one that matches the phone they already use. This guide covers two: Apple's AirTag and Samsung's Galaxy SmartTag2. Apple's four-pack, at $99, costs well over $30.

Bluetooth is a short-range wireless connection between devices. A tracker can only locate an item that is within Bluetooth range of a phone or of a network of nearby devices. If the item is far from both, a tag has little to offer.

Apple's AirTag works with the Find My app on an iPhone or Apple Watch. Apple also offers a feature called Precision Finding, which helps guide you to a nearby tag. According to Apple's own press release, the newest AirTag guides you up to 50 percent farther than the previous generation. Apple also says its speaker is 50 percent louder and can be heard from up to 2x farther. These are Apple's claims about its own product.
Precision Finding is not available everywhere. Apple says it is unavailable where Ultra Wideband, the radio technology behind it, is restricted.
What an item finder cannot do

A tag only helps if it is attached to the thing you lose and your phone is working. It does nothing if the keys are off the keychain. It is not a medical alert or a way for family to check in. For those needs, look at a monitored medical alert system instead. In an emergency, always call 911.
These tags are also not meant for keeping tabs on people. Apple puts it plainly:
"Designed exclusively for tracking objects, and not people or pets." (Apple Newsroom press release, January 2026)

Apple also says its new AirTag includes protections against unwanted tracking, including alerts that work across phone brands. That is meant to protect people from being followed. It can also mean a phone that is not the owner's may receive alerts, so it helps to explain this to whoever receives the gift.

items: Match the phone first. AirTag works with the Find My app on an iPhone or Apple Watch. Samsung's product page does not list which phones the SmartTag2 works with, so confirm that with Samsung or the seller before you buy.
Check for fees. Neither product page below shows a subscription fee, just a one-time price. Still, read the fine print before checkout.
Ask about the battery. Battery details are not on the pages we reviewed, so it is a fair question for the seller: how long does it last, and can it be replaced at home?
Think about loudness. Apple says its newest AirTag has a louder speaker. If you or the recipient have trouble hearing, an audiologist can advise on what sounds are easy to pick up.

Know which features need a newer phone. AirTag's Precision Finding needs an iPhone Air or iPhone 15 or later, not counting iPhone 16e and 17e. On Apple Watch it needs Series 9 or later, or Ultra 2 or later, with watchOS 26.2.1.
Look at the return policy. If the tag turns out not to fit the recipient's phone, you will want an easy return.
Plan the setup. Offer to set it up together, ideally in person.

sections.content: Setting It Up and Using It Well

Setup is the part that makes or breaks this gift. If you can, wrap the tag with a note offering to set it up together. Sit side by side, pair it with the recipient's phone, and attach it to the keys right away.
Then practice once while things are calm, so the steps are easy to remember on a rushed morning. Also walk through the unwanted-tracking alerts so a notification does not come as a surprise.

Pick one item to start with, usually the house or car keys. A wallet or a bag can come next. Apple's four-pack, $99 (list price, November 2026), is an option if you want to cover several things at once.

Apple's AirTag is built for iPhone and Apple Watch. Samsung's page does not list compatibility, though it is generally understood to be meant for Samsung and other Android phones. Confirm with Samsung before buying. If you are unsure what phone a parent has, look in the settings menu or simply ask before you shop.
sections.label: Before You Buy

sections.content: An item finder will not stop anyone from misplacing their keys, but it can turn a ten-minute hunt into a quick search. Choose one that fits the recipient's phone, set it up together, and it makes a small, useful gift.
